title: Has Dark Matter Run Out of Good Ideas?
hook: Two philosophers of physics dissect how dark matter candidates get proposed — and argue the guiding principles that generated WIMPs, axions and the rest may have exhausted their heuristic steam.
key_points: Physicists exploring new territory lean on principles — conservation laws, symmetries, naturalness — as scaffolding for building theories.
The authors call this 'principled inquiry' and treat principles functionally: their force comes from context-dependent reasons to trust them for a purpose.
They analyse four mainstream candidates: supersymmetric WIMPs, axions, sterile neutrinos, and primordial black holes.
All four share a common core of gravitational and non-gravitational principles that defines the dark matter paradigm.
Each departs from orthodox physics differently, and by different amounts — varying degrees of 'minimal mutilation'.
Their diagnosis: the crisis is that the trusted principles may no longer be generating fruitful new options, arguing for more radical exploration.
content_html: Decades of experiments have failed to catch a dark matter particle, and the search has grown philosophically self-conscious. Duerr and Read step back from any particular candidate and ask a methodological question instead: what actually generates dark matter proposals, and is that generator still working?
extra_html:
Their answer starts with principles — conservation laws, symmetries, naturalness arguments, the constraints physicists treat as non-negotiable when venturing into unknown territory. The authors offer a functionalist account: a principle is defined by the job it is meant to do, and its argumentative force reduces to context-sensitive, often tentative reasons for believing it fit for that job. Leaning on well-motivated principles when pushing into new domains is what they call "principled inquiry", and they present it as a historically widespread and methodologically prudent strategy rather than a mistake.

Applying that machinery to four mainstream candidates — supersymmetric WIMPs, axions, sterile neutrinos, and primordial black holes — they argue that the dark matter paradigm is precisely the space of possibilities carved out by a shared cluster of gravitational and non-gravitational principles. Beyond that shared core, each candidate breaks with orthodox physics in a different way and to a different extent, displaying varying degrees of what they call minimal mutilation. Their conclusion is a diagnosis of the field's unease: the crisis is not that dark matter has been refuted, but that the principles researchers have routinely and reasonably relied on may have run out of heuristic steam — which is an argument for exploring ideas that stray considerably further from the cautious path.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: What If Dark Matter Comes in Two Flavors?
related.hook: A single, simple particle can't explain everything odd about dark matter. A new model splits it into two — a heavy kind and a light kind — that quietly sort themselves over cosmic time.

related.title: The Milky Way's Mystery Glow Might Really Be Dark Matter
related.hook: A gamma-ray haze at the galaxy's center has split scientists for years between 'hidden neutron stars' and 'dark matter.' Machine learning just tipped the scales.

related.title: Maybe the Universe Isn't as Finely Tuned as Advertised
related.hook: A review of what happens when you change the constants of nature argues the usual story is overstated: universes with quite different parameters could still make stars, planets, and possibly life.

flashcards.prompt: Which four dark matter approaches do the authors analyse in detail?

choices.text: Supersymmetric WIMPs, axions, sterile neutrinos, and primordial black holes
MOND, modified gravity, extra dimensions, and dark energy
Neutrons, neutrinos, brown dwarfs, and interstellar dust

flashcards.explanation_html: These four are the paper's case studies for showing how each departs from orthodox physics in its own way and to its own degree.

flashcards.prompt: What do Duerr and Read mean by 'minimal mutilation'?
flashcards.back_html: How little of established physics a proposal has to break. Candidates differ in which principles they abandon and how far they stray from orthodoxy.

flashcards.prompt: What is the authors' central worry about the dark matter paradigm?

choices.text: The principles researchers have rationally relied on may have stopped generating fruitful new candidates
That dark matter has been definitively ruled out by direct-detection experiments
That the paradigm never had any principled basis in the first place

flashcards.explanation_html: Their claim is about heuristics running dry, not about a refutation — hence the call to explore ideas that stray further from cautious, principled inquiry.
